steps.title: Open the tool
steps.body: Go to urable-import-tool.vercel.app and bookmark it. Nothing to download or install — it always loads the current version, so just refresh if something looks off. Three boxes: Customers, Products & Services, Jobs History. Drop the shop's export into whichever one matches.
steps.note: Everything is processed inside your own browser. Customer files are never uploaded to a server. The one exception is the direct API import, which writes into the shop's Urable account — which is what you asked it to do.

steps.title: Check what it detected
steps.body: Drop the file and the tool automatically determines the source — here Mobile Tech RX. The right-hand count is what matters: how many customers came through, and how many duplicates it merged. If that number looks wildly wrong, stop and look at the file before going further.

steps.title: Read the preview
steps.body: The first five rows, mapped into the Urable template. Spot-check them: names in the right fields, phone numbers intact, addresses where you expect. The customer list is de-duplicated automatically.

steps.title: Analytics import method
steps.body: Click Download Urable-ready CSV, then upload it through the standard import in Analytics. This is the normal path and the safest one, because a human sees the file before anything is written.
steps.note: The file comes out at exactly 13 columns with no blank rows — nothing past the Item column. That's deliberate: the Urable importer rejects files with stray columns hanging off the end.

steps.title: When the format isn't recognised
steps.body: If the columns are tidy but the system is one the tool hasn't seen, you get Map your columns instead of a preview. This is normal and it's still a two-minute job — you're just telling the tool which column is which.

steps.title: Match the columns
steps.body: Each Urable field gets a dropdown. The tool pre-fills its best guesses and highlights them green — check those first, they're usually right. Set anything irrelevant to — skip —. If the file has one full-name column, pick it for First Name and the tool splits it.

steps.title: Keep everything, then apply
steps.body: Leave Add all unmapped columns to Notes ticked. Anything you didn't map lands in the customer's Notes instead of being thrown away — lead source, tags, account numbers. Then click Apply mapping.
steps.note: Not confident about a mapping? Send the file to Claire instead of guessing. She has a Claude skill that cleans messy lists into the Urable template, and the cleaned file drops straight back into this tool.

steps.title: Review the preview
steps.body: You're back on the standard preview and the flow is identical to Part A — check the rows, then download the CSV or switch to the direct import.

steps.title: Create the API key
steps.body: Connect to their account. In their account go to Settings, scroll to the Developer section, and click + CREATE API KEY.
steps.note: Don't revoke any keys the customer created themselves — only ever add a new one.

steps.title: Name it
steps.body: Call it Urable Import. The name is only a label, but a clear one means the shop knows what it's for later and can revoke it safely once the migration is done.

steps.title: Check off all the boxes
steps.body: Select every scope in the list, then click the green check mark to save.

steps.title: Copy it, then paste it in
steps.body: Copy the key, click Done, and paste it into the import tool. There is no way to see it again once you exit this dialog.
steps.note: Lost it? You can't recover a key, but you can create another in seconds.

steps.title: Paste it into the tool
steps.body: Back in the import tool, switch to the Import directly to Urable tab and paste the key. Make sure the server says Production — it's the default, so it should already be set. Then pick the industry that matches the shop.
steps.note: The key is used for that import only and is never stored. It stays in the browser tab.

steps.title: Test the connection first
steps.body: Check Production is selected, then click Test connection. You want ✓ Connected before going any further — anything else and you stop here, because a bad key wastes the whole run.
steps.note: The result only shows on the button for a few seconds. If you miss it, click again. "Error 400" means the key is wrong.

steps.title: Start it and read the result
steps.body: Check both boxes below the API key field, then Start import and confirm the count when the browser asks. When it finishes you get a plain summary — here 19 customers created, 20 vehicles added. Open the Urable account and spot-check a few before telling the shop it's done.
steps.note: The de-duplication happens only within the file you're importing — it does not check against customers already in their Urable account.

steps.title: Products & services
steps.body: Same flow in the second box. Tiered menus come through grouped — a service priced for Coupe / Sedan / SUV becomes one service with three price points, not three services.

steps.title: Check prices before importing
steps.body: Services vary wildly between systems, so this preview is worth more of your attention than the customer one. Check the prices and the variant labels against the shop's actual menu.

steps.title: Jobs history
steps.body: The third box is the full migration: past jobs with dates, vehicles, services, invoice amounts and historical payments. Note the second figure — total historical payments. Jobs are API import only; there's no CSV path.

steps.title: Review the jobs preview
steps.body: Job numbers, status, customer, vehicle, line items and amounts. Job totals are exact; the split across individual line items is approximate, because most source exports don't carry per-line prices.

steps.title: The one decision that matters
steps.body: Add each historical service to the catalog — leave this unchecked on an account that already has a real service menu. Historical jobs then bill against a single generic "Imported historical service" entry, with the real names preserved in each job's notes, so the shop's live catalog stays clean. Tick it only on a fresh account with no menu yet.
steps.note: Run the customers import first, confirm it looks right, then run jobs. The jobs pass matches existing customers rather than recreating them.

steps.title: Test, then start the jobs run
steps.body: Jobs is API-only, so the same key flow applies: Test connection first, then Start import. A jobs run is much bigger than a customer one — it creates customers, services, vehicles, jobs and payments in a single pass.
steps.note: Leave the tab open and don't navigate away. The import runs from this page — closing it stops the run partway.

steps.title: Watch the phases
steps.body: The bar runs through the phases in order: matching existing records, then customers, services, vehicles, jobs, and finally historical payments. On a real migration this takes a while — 178 operations here.

steps.title: Read the jobs summary
steps.body: Counts for everything created, matched and skipped — and in red, anything that failed with the reason. This real run did 95 jobs created, 3 already imported (skipped), 20 customers, 35 vehicles, 9 historical payments — and 14 jobs failed because those field jobs had no customer address in the source file.
steps.note: Failures are safe: everything else still imported. Fix the underlying data and re-run the same file — the jobs pass skips what it already imported, so only the failures get retried.
